paragraphs: When the first military dispatch came from Beidi, spring rain was still falling in Chang’an.

It reported only that horsemen from Dai had been sighted in Blackwater Valley, that herding families had fled and more than twenty head of cattle had been lost. Following the usual procedure, the Department of State Affairs sent words of reassurance and supplies of bows and arrows, instructing the frontier garrisons to strengthen their patrols. Seven days later a second report arrived. Horsemen from beyond the border had made an incursion, it said, and their numbers were twice those previously reported. Five more days passed before the third dispatch, which claimed that enemy cavalry were moving between two valleys and that perhaps ten thousand riders would soon sweep south.
Each dispatch bore the seal of Fu Luo, Duke of Beihai. The vermilion was fresh and bright, as though the seal had been lifted from blood on the battlefield.

The court began arguing over where reinforcements could be found. Hexi was newly incorporated and armed stragglers still roamed outside Guzang. Northern Dai had only just seen a battle in the snow, and the First Battalion’s troops were scattered among Wuwei, Jincheng and the passes along the road. Murong Chui had scarcely more than seven thousand mobile troops at his disposal. If more men were taken from the frontier, no one could guarantee that some recently conquered town would not abruptly close its gates. An elderly officer of the Military Bureau traced the routes on the map, calculated the distance between relay stations and the carts needed for grain, then said at last, “We have soldiers who can march. The grain to feed them is not where the soldiers are.”

Fu Luo soon submitted a petition for troops. Respectfully phrased, it said that the commanderies of Beidi lacked defenders and asked permission to recruit fifteen thousand men. The older military rolls would be submitted for verification by the Department of State Affairs, rations would come from government granaries, and the court could send an assistant commander to supervise. He did not even ask for the return of his former personal troops. He said only that families along the border feared abduction and plunder: without soldiers to protect their fields, they would produce no grain for the state after autumn.

When the petition reached court, several elderly generals praised the duke’s grasp of the larger situation. Lü Polou spoke with particular feeling. “Life on the frontier is hard. You gentlemen gaze at a map in Chang’an, and someone out there loses another night’s sleep. His Lordship is willing to submit the new recruits’ names to the court. Why continue to suspect him?”
“Providing men is one thing; handing over command is another,” Fu Rong said. “Whose orders will those fifteen thousand obey in the days to come?”
“The Heavenly King’s, of course.”
“And if the Heavenly King’s order takes twenty days to reach the border from Chang’an?”

Lü Polou could not answer. Fu Hong was holding all three dispatches. He had already marked on the map the places where the enemy riders were said to have appeared. After glancing at his father, he finally stepped forward and said that he favored recruitment, provided that the military register, grain supplies and the commander’s authority were administered separately.
Several men in the hall were surprised. The crown prince had answered Fu Luo firmly at the spring banquet. Now he was prepared to give him troops.
“The families outside the passes are suffering,” Fu Hong said. “They should not have to wait while the court and the imperial clan decide which side has prevailed.”

Fu Jian told him to explain his proposal in detail. Fu Hong suggested that the commanderies recruit separately, and that the new men be verified against household registers before assignment to their units. Government granaries would issue pay and grain by name. Any movement of more than a thousand men would require the command tally to be checked jointly with the court-appointed deputy. Fu Rong added that the principal commander could not appoint every officer; the Military Bureau must at least review the home districts and ranks of junior officers.
“If every soldier obeys only paper, will they fight when enemy cavalry arrive?” Lü Polou demanded.

Fu Hong faced the old general. “They will fight. There must be a commander in battle. What the court must be able to establish is whether that same army can be counted back into the registers afterward.”
Fu Jian did not approve the plan immediately. He summoned Fu Rong and the crown prince into a side hall, then asked, “Could Chang Xuan go?”

Chang Xuan had once managed muster rolls and grain escorts in the Central Army. In seniority he ranked beneath even one of Fu Luo’s old commandants, yet he had never miscounted a single supply wagon. During the autumn floods he had kept the grain safe at a relay station in Hedong, choosing to quarrel with his commander until both were red in the face rather than release a cart without a verified order. Fu Rong said that if they sent him, Fu Luo might be furious but could hardly claim the court had appointed a rival general to take away his command.

Fu Jian wrote his approval on the back of the petition. Beidi might recruit fifteen thousand men; the Department of State Affairs would verify their names and issue grain. Chang Xuan would serve as deputy commander, carrying one half of the divided command tally. The new units must no longer use the old names of the ducal household. Their soldiers would be known simply as the Beidi Border Guard.

As the edict passed through the palace gate, Fu Hong hurried after the Secretariat clerk escorting the messenger and asked him to add one item to the transfer register: the actual quantity of grain dispatched by the Department of State Affairs and the date it reached Beidi must be reported every ten days. The clerk agreed, then asked why he was so urgent.
“I fear the frontier will run out of grain while the accounts are still arguing over whose army it is,” Fu Hong replied.

Fu Luo received the edict, prostrated himself in thanks according to ritual, and at once gave a banquet for the messenger. The senior steward of his residence remained at table far into the night. Only after the outsiders had left did he voice the question he had kept to himself for days. “Does Your Lordship truly intend to let Chang Xuan come and inspect us?”
“It is an edict from the Heavenly King. How could I refuse?”
“What if he traces every man who served in the duke’s old army?”

Fu Luo poured his wine into an earthen bowl beside the table and did not answer at once. On the parade ground in Beidi, men from his old following still gathered in the evenings to shoot arrows. Row upon row of feathered shafts stood in the targets, like a flock of wild geese that had flown far away years ago but never quite scattered.
“Where do those men live now?” he asked.
“Most in the counties of Beidi. Some herd horses, some cultivate land, others work in the residence. When the former rolls were abolished, Your Lordship gave them travel money.”
“Then they are people of Beidi,” Fu Luo said. “The Heavenly King has authorized us to recruit the people of Beidi to defend the border. They may join as well.”

The steward understood. A man could change his entry in the military registers without changing what he called his commander. Scattered among the counties, Fu Luo’s old soldiers could return as separate recruits. On paper they would no longer appear to form an army of the ducal household; gathered on the parade ground, they would still have the same faces.

At dawn the recruiting drums sounded from the commandery city as far as the market outside its walls. Grain would be issued monthly, and recruits’ families would be exempted from a year of labor service. Tenant farmers from the border estates came with knives, poor men led lean horses, and veterans who had once fought under Fu Luo came as well. One old soldier was missing his left ear. The recruiting clerk complained that he was too old, but Fu Luo happened by, examined his fingers, and recognized a smith who had lost the tips to frostbite while guarding a ditch years before.
“Can you still swing a hammer?” Fu Luo asked.
“I can.”
“Then repair crossbows. You needn’t race the younger men.”

The veteran bowed, tears reddening his eyes, and the clerk had to enter his name under the skilled laborers. Others saw the exchange and said that the Duke of Beihai still remembered his old companions. On the strength of those words, some began addressing one another by the titles they had once held in his personal army.

Fu Luo forbade the old banners in public, but did not forbid former followers to recognize one another. Several officers attached to his household quietly stitched black thread into their wristguards. During drills they need only raise a hand to see which men would still obey the old command names. At first scarcely a dozen copied the black stitching. Within ten days soldiers in other units had begun to do the same. By the time the senior steward heard of it, hundreds of men had black thread sewn into their guards. He did not include the matter in the dispatch he sent to Chang’an.

News of the recruiting reached Anding quickly. Shopkeeper Shi visited Lei Edi with contracts from three horse farms, asking to purchase eight hundred horses. They were bought in three lots, their consignees changed along the route. Only in the end did the government purchase them as mounts for the Beidi units.
When Lei Edi saw that neither Fu Luo’s name nor Yao Chang’s appeared in the contracts, he laughed. “You merchants are frightened the horses might recognize their master.”

Shi replied that horses recognized grass and water, and went wherever someone paid to take them. Lei Edi did not entirely believe him, but sold the horses nevertheless. They were thin after winter. Of the eight hundred driven on the long journey, many fell ill or were requisitioned by other garrisons. Only six hundred and forty-seven reached Beidi and could be entered on its military lists. The shipping documents nevertheless recorded the full prices, with each seal clearly impressed. The men of Anding could not see the purchasers’ intentions, nor could the men of Beidi discern the old Qiang alliance from the cargo manifests.

In Chang’an, Yao Chang glanced over a leather merchant’s account and saw payments to three horse farms at the end. He told his steward to retain it. When someone asked whether he had arranged business for the Duke of Beihai, he replied, “Beidi needs horses, and merchants sell them. Must they ask the Right Guard’s permission as well?”

In the fifth month Murong Chui returned to Chang’an from northern Dai. The garrisons of Hexi remained under separate commanders; he brought back only his mobile force and men whose wounds had healed enough for them to rejoin it. Some had wanted to welcome him by Ba Bridge, but the general refused the decorated canopy. The soldiers marched into the capital with dust still on their helmets. Their wagons carried armor plates belonging to the dead and registers of rewards not yet paid. Fu Hong met the army outside the city, ordered hot food for the wounded from the grain office, then accompanied Murong Chui to the palace to surrender his command tally.
Fu Jian looked at the general’s face and asked, “Is any ash left from the Yan flag you burned on the snowfield?”
“The snow buried it. Once the spring water melts through, I doubt anyone could find it.”
“Do you regret its loss?”
“I do.”
“Do you regret burning it?”
Murong Chui paused. “It is not yet time for regret.”

Fu Jian looked at the man who had once stood in the royal court of Yan. He knew there was an old wound within him that no one had the right to touch, and he asked no more. Instead, he gave Murong Chui the three dispatches from Beidi.

Murong Chui first checked the place names, then the dates each message had been sent. Finally he called for a map and the previous year’s records of grazing in Beidi. No one in the hall spoke. Only the faint sound of paper turning could be heard.

“Blackwater Valley cannot hold three thousand horses for three days,” he said. “The spring grass has not yet grown. What would they eat? The second report says the enemy crossed two frozen rivers in two days. The ice broke early this spring. Taking another route would need five days—unless someone has three thousand horses that can fly.”
“How many men of Dai are there, then?” Fu Jian asked.

“There are certainly enough to make repeated raids along the frontier. I have seen no evidence that they can assemble ten thousand horsemen at once. Last year’s battle in the snow cost them many men and horses. If ten thousand riders were truly coming, they would leave great supplies of fodder, horse dung and trampled pastures along their route. Not one of the three dispatches mentions any of that.”
“Fu Luo has defended the frontier for ten years. Can he not see it?”
Murong Chui closed the reports and was slow to reply. Fu Jian noticed a fresh wound across his fingertips and did not repeat the question.
“Should I withdraw the order authorizing recruitment?”

“If Your Majesty withdraws it now, those who genuinely defend the border may be driven into the Duke of Beihai’s camp as well,” Murong Chui replied. “I ask only that you see whether Chang Xuan can enter the central camp with his half of the tally. If he can, there is still room to speak.”
“And if they will not let him through?”
“Then the Duke of Beihai must explain in person why the Heavenly King’s half-tally carries less authority than his spoken word.”

By this time Beidi had recruited thirteen thousand six hundred and seventy-two men. On arriving, Chang Xuan paid the customary call at the duke’s residence and accepted Fu Luo’s hospitality. Early the next morning, however, he sent the wooden muster tokens to the units, ordering every man to present himself by name at the parade ground north of the city within three days.

Just over three thousand came the first day, and more than two thousand the second. At the end of the third day the total was still below seven thousand. The missing men were said to be watching beacon towers, stationed in mountain valleys or sick at home. Yet the grain officials’ daily issues had been calculated for more than thirteen thousand men, down to the last measure.

Chang Xuan did not grow angry in front of the soldiers. He questioned those who had appeared, one after another. One man claimed to be twenty-two, though half his temples were gray. Another did not recognize the village written as his birthplace. A young recruit admitted he was serving under his brother’s name: his brother’s leg was ruined, and he was taking the grain and guarding the pass in his place. Chang Xuan’s accompanying scribes worked through the night copying four books of discrepancies, raising blisters on the fingers that gripped their brushes.

A Beidi commandant slammed the table. What did a man’s birthplace or age matter when the enemy arrived? If he could kill, he was good enough. Chang Xuan handed him a grain voucher. “When that man dies, whose household receives the relief grain? You call him Zhang San, the government book says Li Si. Where is the old mother waiting at home supposed to go to claim her rations?”
The commandant had no answer, though his face remained red with anger.

Chang Xuan turned to the horses. Six hundred and forty-seven had only recently entered the stables, and not all had saddles. The cargo records nevertheless bore seals from three horse farms in Anding. He ordered the supply officers to seal the sales contracts together with the wooden inspection tallies for each horse. An official protested that the frontier had needed mounts urgently and a twenty-percent price increase was unavoidable. Chang Xuan replied merely that the price could be reviewed later, but the horses delivered must be inspected one by one.

On the third day Chang Xuan met Fu Luo and requested that the appointment of officers to the new units be suspended. Fu Luo poured tea for him personally. “If the riders from Dai cross the border tomorrow, which soldier without an official seal shall we send to meet them?”
“Let temporary commanders serve as before. Grant the seals when the registers have been verified.”

“*Temporary* is an easy word to say. Men must go out on watch tonight. If an order comes from their commander and they must first ask where he received his seal, who will gather the bodies afterward?”

“Your Lordship has defended the frontier for many years. You understand these things better than I,” Chang Xuan answered. “I ask only this: how have more than two thousand men of the old ducal army all found their way into the new units? They have broken no law. Yet why can commandants sent by the court not even change the night-watch drum when they enter the camp?”
The tea trembled in Fu Luo’s cup. He set it down gently. “Does Deputy Chang think the soldiers of Beidi acknowledge no one but me?”
“I want them to acknowledge the court’s orders as well.”
“Then let Chang’an prove it can shield them from arrows,” Fu Luo said. “Go back. I shall still let you inspect the accounts. As for command in the camps, we will discuss it after the enemy has gone.”

Chang Xuan left the residence. Rainwater was falling in a straight thread from the eaves. His attendant asked why he did not withdraw to Chang’an. He had been here only a few days, Chang Xuan replied; the grain had not even been fully counted. How could he abandon the people here? He then divided the records of false or mismatched registrations into three packets, sent them toward the capital by separate men on different relay roads, and wrote a private letter to Fu Rong describing the actual situation at the camp gates and granaries.

Several days later he carried his half of the command tally to Beidi’s central camp. The officer guarding the gate said that the Duke of Beihai had gone out to inspect the passes and had not returned. Outsiders could not enter the armory.

Chang Xuan waited outside the tent until sunset. Cold wind swept along the city wall, and the flag rope kept striking the pole. He asked whether the half-tally given him by His Majesty counted as an army credential. The commandant replied, “For moving soldiers, yes. To inspect the armory you need the duke’s order in person.”
Chang Xuan argued not a word. Back at his lodgings he wrote a report. He understood now that another word would not get him through the gate.

That night a message arrived: riders from Dai had been spotted near a northwestern beacon station. Fu Luo requested the deputy to accompany a party to verify the sighting before the troops were sent out. Chang Xuan read the letter twice. Its timing struck him as too convenient. His guards urged him not to go. He replied that if he stayed, tomorrow’s dispatch would say the deputy had flinched before the enemy. And if there truly were raiders, how could he answer to the court for neglecting the border?
“Leave the half-tally here and seal every record of a false registration,” he told his closest attendant. “If I have not returned by dawn, send them at once to the Lord of Yangping.”

He rode out with only twelve guards. Rain had fallen in the night, and hoofbeats had churned the narrow road to ruin. As they entered the river valley, three torches appeared ahead. The men holding them claimed to have been sent by the Duke of Beihai to guide the way. Chang Xuan asked where the three hundred riders from Dai had entered the valley. The answer was simply that the beacon tower lay ahead.

Chang Xuan bent low in the saddle and scooped up a handful of mud. There were no fresh tracks from a large body of hostile horsemen; instead several wagon ruts turned away toward the slope. He drew rein at once and ordered his men back to the city. The words had scarcely left his mouth when the torches went out and bowstrings sounded together from the darkness on either side.

The first arrow pierced a guard’s throat. Another man fell with his horse into the mud. Chang Xuan drew his blade and shouted for the survivors to hold the mouth of the valley. The men on the slopes had wrapped themselves in black cloth. They displayed no banners and did not utter even a battle cry. They meant to surround and kill the dozen or so men in silence and haste.

A long spear felled Chang Xuan’s horse. He rolled in the muddy water, seized a guard’s belt and thrust a short letter he had already written into the man’s hands. “Go by the river. Take this to the Lord of Yangping.”
The man refused to leave him. Chang Xuan shoved him away. “If you stay, everyone who dies here tonight will have died for nothing.”

The guard plunged into the icy river. Two men pursued him, only to be stopped by Chang Xuan and another of his soldiers. Reeds rustled on the opposite bank, then fell silent. In the valley, blades were still flashing. Wounded in the left shoulder, Chang Xuan staggered back against a stone. A man on the slope shouted, “Deputy Chang! Throw down your blade and His Lordship will spare you!”
The speaker fell silent the instant the words escaped him. Chang Xuan recognized his accent—and the voice that had barred his entry at the camp gate.
“You dare invoke him out here,” Chang Xuan said with a breathless laugh. “Why not say it to his face?”
Another spear struck. He caught it on his blade, chipping the edge. Several attackers rushed him together. The last spark fell into the mud and never shone again.

At dawn Beidi reported that Chang Xuan had been ambushed by riders from Dai. Eleven of his twelve guards had died; the last was missing. When Fu Luo arrived at the valley, the bodies had not yet all been gathered. Half Chang Xuan’s face lay buried in the mud. His right hand clutched the hilt of a notched sword, the joints already stiff.

The senior steward of the ducal residence reported cautiously that the men sent out in the night had all returned to camp, save for the guard who had gone into the river. No one knew whether he lived. Fu Luo wheeled around. “When did I order you to kill him?”
The steward dropped to his knees. “Your Lordship said only that he must not be allowed to continue his inspections. The men in camp feared he would send the old registers back to Chang’an…”

Fu Luo kicked over a basin of mud beside him. “If you kill him, can you bring back the accounts already sent away? Chang Xuan came here under the Heavenly King’s orders. He died on my land. What am I supposed to say?”
The steward struck his forehead against the ground. “For now we say he was attacked by riders from Dai. If we find the missing guard, give him money and send him somewhere far away.”
Fu Luo looked at the blood on the earth. A long time passed before he spoke. “Do you think everyone can be bought?”

He crouched beside Chang Xuan and lifted the dead man’s half-buried face out of the mud. He had been no more than a man who wrote names in ledgers, and his features had little of a great general’s bearing. Yet now they were harder to conceal than any military dispatch. Fu Luo remembered Fu Jian’s question at the spring banquet: *How many soldiers do you want?* At the time he had believed that if he could hold Beidi, one day his cousin would admit he was still indispensable.

Fu Luo ordered Chang Xuan laid out with the honors due a deputy commander and his remains sent to the capital. The dispatch prepared for Chang’an still said that riders from Dai had killed him in an ambush. When it was written, Fu Luo looked at his seal. The heavy piece of bronze had become strangely difficult to hold.
“Will the Eastern Pass remain open?” the steward asked. “The Lord of Yangping has already passed Anding.”
“Close it,” Fu Luo said. “Say enemy riders have not yet been cleared out. Every envoy must have his identity checked before entering.”
“Even if it is the Lord of Yangping?”
Fu Luo let his gaze rest a moment on Chang Xuan’s coffin. “Especially him. I will see him when I have decided what to do.”

The surviving guard had drifted in the river for half the night, an arrow lodged in his left shoulder, before herdsmen dragged him into their hut. He burned with fever for two days, then hauled himself, still ill, to Fu Rong’s army. The short letter had been hidden beneath the sole of his boot and was nearly falling to pieces from the water. Fu Rong unfolded it. The ink slanted across the paper:
*The rolls are false. The camp gates are barred. Those who kill me cannot be men of Dai.*

After reading, Fu Rong slipped the letter into his case for imperial edicts and ordered that the wounded guard be escorted to Chang’an at once to testify. Others advised him to halt and await fresh orders from the court. He shook his head. “Chang Xuan sent these lines so I would not believe the dispatches alone. If I do not go, who will ask what happened to him?”

Two days later the Eastern Pass rose on the horizon. Its towers were high, the gate passage deep, and the shadow of its battlements stretched across the dusty yellow road. Qin banners still flew above the walls, and the archers stood in ordered ranks. Fu Rong had the Heavenly King’s ceremonial staff raised and three times formally requested that the gates be opened. Not even a footstep sounded from within. After a while, a reply bearing the Duke of Beihai’s seal was shot out in a bamboo tube and landed before his horse. It said hostile riders had slipped across the frontier, and that the Lord of Yangping would be admitted when the matter was resolved.
Fu Rong gripped the bamboo tube and looked up from his saddle. “Does the Duke of Beihai know who I am?”
“He does,” the commandant on the wall replied.
“Does he know whose edict I carry?”
“He does.”
“Then open the gates.”

The commandant said nothing. Behind him, the archers’ fingers went white as they slowly drew their bowstrings tight. Fu Rong could make out several familiar old Di soldiers upon the walls. Years before they had defended Guanzhong beside him. Now they avoided his eyes.
“In whose hands did Chang Xuan die?” he asked.
“Riders from Dai.”
“Then hand over the riders who killed him.”
“They have escaped.”
“Let me inside to investigate.”
Again came the answer from the wall: “The frontier situation remains uncertain. The gates cannot be opened.”

Fu Rong was silent for a moment. He ordered the Heavenly King’s staff held higher. Behind him two thousand men of the Central Army placed their hands upon their swords, but not one drew first. He knew they were too few to storm the fortress, and he would not have Qin soldiers slaughter Qin soldiers that night. Yet if an imperial edict could become worthless paper before the Eastern Pass, what would happen at the next city?

Toward evening a new military flag was raised above the gate tower. Its cloth was white, bearing two characters in black ink: *Beidi*. It had been cut to the pattern of the army banners newly prescribed in Chang’an. It carried neither the Fu clan’s princely title nor any old family emblem. The wind stretched the cloth straight, while inside the gate one heavy wooden bar after another dropped into place.

Listening to their dull blows, Fu Rong remembered the night Wang Meng died, when the palace gates were locked. Then it had been the emperor inside and the generals outside. Now he stood outside with the emperor’s edict, and the men within wore Qin armor.

The dusk thickened, and cold dust lifted from the official road. Fu Rong neither lowered the ceremonial staff nor ordered an assault. He had his soldiers pitch camp beyond the range of the fortress bows, sent an urgent report to Chang’an, then told his chief registrar to write Chang Xuan’s name, clearly and carefully, on the very first line.
